summary: Reviewed the DVPWA (dvpwa / 'sqli') aiohttp application: DAO layer, views, routes, auth utilities, middlewares, Jinja2 integration, config, SQL migrations and templates. The application is intentionally insecure and contains a classic, unauthenticated SQL injection, global disabling of HTML autoescaping (stored XSS), disabled CSRF enforcement, weak MD5 password hashing, non-HttpOnly session cookies, and broad missing authorization on state-changing endpoints. Overall risk is critical: an unauthenticated attacker can inject SQL and persist XSS. Coverage was the full Python source, templates, config and migrations; static vendored JS/CSS and fonts were not reviewed.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement with Python string interpolation ('%(name)s' % {'name': name}) instead of a parameterized query. The name value is attacker-controlled: views.students (sqli/views.py:54-57) reads data['name'] from an unauthenticated POST to /students/ (route sqli/routes.py:14) and passes it straight to Student.create with no validation. An attacker can submit a name such as x'); DROP TABLE students;-- or a stacked/sub-select payload to read, modify or destroy any data in the database and, via PostgreSQL, potentially escalate further. This is the only DAO method using string formatting; all others correctly parameterize.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name}); cur.execute(q)  <- name flows from request.post()['name'] in views.students (sqli/views.py:57) with no sanitization and no auth check.
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query: cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never build SQL with % / f-strings on user input.

findings.title: Global Jinja2 autoescape disabled enabling stored XSS via review text and student names
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so all template variables are rendered as raw HTML unless an explicit |e filter is used. User-controlled values are rendered without escaping, e.g. review.review_text at sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22 and student name at sqli/templates/students.jinja2:16 and course.title/description at course.jinja2:14-15. An attacker can POST a review containing <script>...</script> to /courses/{id}/review (unauthenticated) which is then stored and executed in every visitor's browser (stored XSS). Combined with the non-HttpOnly session cookie, this allows session hijacking.
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, ..., autoescape=False) at sqli/app.py:35; sink example: '{{ review.review_text }}' at sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22, value created from unsanitized data['review_text'] in views.review (sqli/views.py:121-129).
findings.recommendation: Set autoescape=True (the Jinja2 default) and only use the |safe filter on values known to be safe. Remove autoescape=False.

findings.title: CSRF enforcement middleware disabled application-wide
findings.description: The csrf_middleware (sqli/middlewares.py:25-38) that validates the _csrf_token on POST requests is commented out of the middleware chain. Although forms embed csrf_token() and a token is generated by csrf_processor, nothing ever verifies it. All state-changing POST endpoints (create student, create course, create review, evaluate/assign marks, login, logout) are therefore vulnerable to cross-site request forgery; an attacker can auto-submit forms from a malicious page to create records or (as admin) assign marks on behalf of a logged-in victim.
findings.evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware,\n error_middleware] at sqli/app.py:25-29 — csrf_middleware is commented out; validation logic exists but is unreachable (sqli/middlewares.py:25-38).
findings.recommendation: Enable csrf_middleware in the middleware list and ensure every POST form submits a valid token; reject mismatches with 403.

findings.title: Missing authorization checks on state-changing endpoints (evaluate, create student/course/review)
findings.description: The evaluate handler assigns marks to students but performs no authentication or authorization check; the @authorize decorator exists (sqli/utils/auth.py:12-23) but is applied only to logout. The UI hides the evaluate form behind auth_user.is_admin (sqli/templates/course.jinja2:41), but the handler itself is reachable by anyone via POST /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id}. The same missing-auth pattern applies to the mutating handlers students (POST, sqli/views.py:54-57), courses (POST, sqli/views.py:86-90) and review (POST, sqli/views.py:119-130): any unauthenticated client can create students, courses, reviews and grade students. This is a broken access control / privilege escalation flaw.
findings.evidence: async def evaluate(request) at sqli/views.py:134 has no @authorize and no user check before Mark.create (sqli/views.py:151-152); contrast logout which is decorated with @authorize() at sqli/views.py:156.
findings.recommendation: Apply @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to evaluate and @authorize() to the other mutating handlers (or add explicit role checks), so that privileged actions require the appropriate authenticated role.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5
findings.description: User.check_password compares the stored hash to md5(password). Passwords are stored as unsalted MD5 (see migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10-13 which seed md5('superadmin') etc.). MD5 is fast and broken: stored hashes are trivially cracked with rainbow tables/GPU, and identical passwords produce identical hashes. If the database is read (e.g. via the SQL injection above), all account passwords including the superadmin's are recoverable.
findings.evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest() at sqli/dao/user.py:41; seeds use md5('superadmin') at migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10.
findings.recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hash (bcrypt, scrypt or argon2) via a vetted library, and migrate existing hashes on next login. Use constant-time comparison.

findings.title: Session cookie set without HttpOnly flag
findings.description: RedisStorage is created with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable from JavaScript. Combined with the stored XSS enabled by autoescape=False, an attacker's injected script can read document.cookie and exfiltrate the victim's session, enabling full account takeover (including the admin). No Secure flag is set either.
findings.recommendation: Use httponly=True (the default) and secure=True for the session cookie; serve over HTTPS.

findings.title: Application runs with aiohttp debug mode enabled
findings.description: The Application is constructed with debug=True unconditionally. In production this enables verbose diagnostics/warnings and can lead to information disclosure of internal state and stack details. It is hardcoded rather than driven by configuration.
findings.recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False in production deployments.

findings.title: Hardcoded default database credentials in config
findings.description: The committed configuration uses default PostgreSQL credentials (user postgres / password post****). This file is the default config loaded by app init (default_config='./config/dev.yaml', sqli/app.py:18). If this config is reused beyond local dev, the default superuser credentials provide trivial database access. These look like development defaults rather than a unique production secret, but default/weak DB credentials should still be avoided.
findings.evidence: db.user: postgres / db.password: post**** at config/dev.yaml:2-3; loaded as default_config in sqli/app.py:18.
findings.recommendation: Load DB credentials from environment/secrets, use non-default strong credentials, and keep real credentials out of version control.

findings.title: Outdated dependencies with known vulnerabilities (aiohttp 3.5.3, PyYAML 3.13)
findings.description: Several pinned dependencies are old and carry published CVEs. aiohttp==3.5.3 (requirements.txt:3) predates fixes for HTTP request smuggling and open-redirect issues (e.g. CVE-2021-21330 and later advisories) resolved in 3.7.x/3.8.x. PyYAML==3.13 (requirements.txt:15) is affected by CVE-2020-14343 (arbitrary code execution via yaml.load/full_load) fixed in 5.4. These are reachable in a running deployment via the HTTP stack and config parsing respectively.
findings.evidence: aiohttp==3.5.3 (requirements.txt:3); pyyaml==3.13 (requirements.txt:15); jinja2==2.10 (requirements.txt:11) is also old.
findings.recommendation: Upgrade to current supported releases (aiohttp >=3.9, PyYAML >=6, Jinja2 >=3.1) and run pip-audit regularly in CI.
